L8@P0: The leaves of the carnivorous plant Venus flytrap, Dionaea
L9@P0: muscipula (Dionaea) close rapidly to capture insect prey. The
L10@P0: closure response usually requires two successive mechanical
L11@P0: stimuli to sensory hairs on the leaf blade within approximately
L12@P0: 30 s (refs. 1–4). An unknown biological system in Dionaea is
L13@P0: thought to memorize the first stimulus and transduce the
L14@P0: signal from the sensory hair to the leaf blade2
L15@P0: . Here, we link
L16@P0: signal memory to calcium dynamics using transgenic Dionaea
L17@P0: expressing a Ca2+ sensor. Stimulation of a sensory hair caused
L18@P0: an increase in cytosolic Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]cyt) starting
L19@P0: in the sensory hair and spreading to the leaf blade. A second
L20@P0: stimulus increased [Ca2+]cyt to an even higher level, meeting a
L21@P0: threshold that is correlated to the leaf blade closure. Because
L22@P0: [Ca2+]cyt gradually decreased after the first stimulus, the
L23@P0: [Ca2+]cyt increase induced by the second stimulus was insufficient to meet the putative threshold for movement after
L24@P0: about 30 s. The Ca2+ wave triggered by mechanical stimulation moved an order of magnitude faster than that induced by
L25@P0: wounding in petioles of Arabidopsis thaliana5
L26@P0:  and Dionaea. The
L27@P0: capacity for rapid movement has evolved repeatedly in flowering plants. This study opens a path to investigate the role of
L28@P0: Ca2+ in plant movement mechanisms and their evolution.
L29@P0: Plants have evolved a variety of mechanisms that ‘remember’
L30@P0: external stimuli as part of numerous processes, including acclimation to harsh environments, systemic acquired resistance to
L31@P0: pathogens and vernalization6
L32@P0: . In the short-term memory system of
L33@P0: Dionaea (Fig. 1a), the second stimulus can be to any of the leaf ’s six
L34@P0: sensory hairs (Fig. 1b), regardless of which hair received the first
L35@P0: stimulus2
L36@P0: . Previous studies showed that mechanical stimulation of a
L37@P0: sensory hair generates action potentials that propagate to both lobes
L38@P0: of the leaf7,8
L39@P0: . Other studies have shown that leaf closure is blocked
L40@P0: by Ca2+ channel inhibitors that should inhibit increase of the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration ([Ca2+]cyt) of leaf cells, emphasizing the
L41@P0: importance of Ca2+ in the response9–11. On the basis of these results,
L42@P0: the mechanism of Dionaea memory has been proposed to be as follows10,12: (1) [Ca2+]cyt increases during excitation; (2) [Ca2+]cyt or the
L43@P0: concentration of some Ca2+-activated regulatory molecules must
L44@P0: reach a threshold for movement; (3) a single action potential is not
L45@P0: enough to increase [Ca2+]cyt to the threshold and at least two action
L46@P0: potentials are necessary to trigger movement; (4) [Ca2+]cyt decreases
L47@P0: after the first stimulus and after 30 s does not reach the threshold
L48@P0: even with a second stimulus. This hypothesis has not been directly
L49@P0: tested because of the lack of a method for spatiotemporal calcium
L50@P0: monitoring in Dionaea.
L51@P0: Since transformation of Dionaea has not been reported, to
L52@P0: observe spatiotemporal cytosolic [Ca2+] changes in Dionaea,
L53@P0: we set out to transform excised leaves with Agrobacterium carrying a construct for constitutive expression of sGFP (refs. 13–15;
L54@P0: pSB111U2-sGFP; Supplementary Fig. 1a). On the basis of the number of leaves expressing sGFP, etiolated leaves had a significantly
L55@P0: higher transformation rate (97% (n=96)) than did non-etiolated
L56@P0: leaves (46% (n=91)) (two-tail P=4.8×10–12 by Fisher’s exact
L57@P0: test). Furthermore, shoot regeneration rates from etiolated leaves
L58@P0: were significantly higher under continuous dark conditions (55%
L59@P0: (n=60)) than under continuous light conditions (27% (n=60))
L60@P0: (two-tail P=0.0028 by Fisher’s exact test). From 77 excised etiolated
L61@P0: leaves, we obtained seven transgenic plants that constitutively and
L62@P0: ubiquitously expressed sGFP (Supplementary Fig. 2).
L63@P0: Using the same procedures, we next produced plants transformed with a construct for constitutive expression of the calcium
L64@P0: sensor protein GCaMP6f, which contains a cpEGFP fluorescent
L65@P0: moiety14,16 (pSB111U2-GCaMP6f; Supplementary Fig. 1b). Five
L66@P0: transgenic plants were obtained from 245 excised etiolated leaves.
L67@P0: When non-excised leaves of GCaMP6f-transgenic Dionaea were
L68@P0: placed on ice, cpEGFP fluorescence increased in both leaf lobes and
L69@P0: petioles (Fig. 1c), as reported for cold-treated leaves of Arabidopsis
L70@P0: thaliana17. Cytosolic localization of cpEGFP fluorescence was
L71@P0: observed in a cut leaf blade (Supplementary Fig. 3).
L72@P0: We mechanically stimulated a sensory hair of GCaMP6f Dionaea
L73@P0: and observed that cpEGFP fluorescence increased within 0.02 s at
L74@P0: the base of the hair (Fig. 2a), where the sensory cells that generate action potentials are located7
L75@P0: . Over time, fluorescence intensity
L76@P0: continued to increase in the sensory hair (Fig. 2a) and fluorescence
L77@P0: spread radially from the sensory hair to the surrounding leaf tissue
L78@P0: (Fig. 2c,d, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2).
L79@P0: There are non-pigmented glands and pigmented digestive glands on
L80@P0: the leaf blade2
L81@P0: . The increase of fluorescence intensity was detected
L82@P0: in the former glands but not in the latter. Fluorescence also propagated from one lobe of the leaf to the other (Fig. 2e,f left, Extended
L83@P0: Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Video 3). In the abaxial view, fluorescence was not detected in the midrib (Fig. 2f right). This suggests
L84@P0: that fluorescence is propagated in the epidermis and/or parenchyma
L85@P0: adaxial to the midrib but not in the midrib and tissue surrounding
L86@P0: the midrib, both of which are connected to the petiole (Fig. 2f,g).

L88@P0: in transgenic Venus flytrap

L92@P1: This is consistent with the observation that fluorescence did not
L93@P1: propagate into the petiole (Fig. 2f).
L94@P1: We could not localize fluorescence to specific cells because of
L95@P1: the difficulty of observing intact cells deep within the leaf and the
L96@P1: need to avoid wound-induced fluorescence that would be caused
L97@P1: by physical dissection (Supplementary Fig. 3). The fluorescence
L98@P1: signal extended laterally as far as the area where secondary leaf
L99@P1: veins, which run perpendicularly from a primary vein in the midrib
L100@P1: toward the leaf edges, begin to branch and merge with neighbouring veins (Fig. 2h). This was the furthest lateral spread observed on
L101@P1: both the adaxial and abaxial sides of the leaf (Fig. 2f).
L102@P1: The average propagation velocity in the medial direction
L103@P1: (53±8.2mms–1 (mean±s.e.m., n=8 leaves)) was faster than that in
L104@P1: the lateral direction (20±6.8mms–1 (mean±s.e.m., n=8 leaves)).
L105@P1: Average velocities in the proximal and distal directions were similar
L106@P1: to that in the lateral direction (23±3.2mms–1 (mean±s.e.m., n=8
L107@P1: leaves) and 21±3.2mms–1 (mean±s.e.m., n=8 leaves), respectively) (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). The velocity did not
L108@P1: change when the fluorescence crossed a leaf vein or the midrib
L109@P1: (Supplementary Video 3). The Ca2+ wave velocities resulting from
L110@P1: stimulation of a sensory hair and those caused by wounding to the
L111@P1: leaf blade were not distinguished (Extended Data Figs. 3c and 4,
L112@P1: Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Video 4). It should be
L113@P1: noted that similar action potentials are produced in response to
L114@P1: mechanical stimulation and wounding18.
L115@P1: Fluorescence of unstimulated sensory hairs increased when
L116@P1: the wave front reached them (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Video
L117@P1: 1). This is consistent with the observation that leaf closure can be
L118@P1: induced with a second stimulus to any sensory hair, not only the
L119@P1: one that received the first stimulus. It is noteworthy that the Ca2+
L120@P1: wave velocities resulting from stimulation of a sensory hair as well
L121@P1: as those caused by wounding to the leaf blade are approximately
L122@P1: 50 to 20 times faster than those caused by wounding to petioles in
L123@P1: A. thaliana (1.089mms–1) (ref. 5
L124@P1: ) and in Dionaea (1.2±0.17mms–1
L125@P1: (mean±s.e.m., n=5 leaves)) (Extended Data Figs. 3d and 5 and
L126@P1: Supplementary Video 5).
L127@P1: We next observed Ca2+ dynamics following a second stimulus.
L128@P1: The second stimulus further increased the signal intensity of the
L129@P1: stimulated sensory hair (Fig. 2b), then propagated radially to mostly
L130@P1: the same area as the first stimulus did and the leaf closed (Fig. 2c,
L131@P1: Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Video 1). Average propagation velocities for the second stimulus were approximately two to
L132@P1: three times faster than those for the first stimulus in all four directions (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 3b, Supplementary Table 1 and
L133@P1: Supplementary Video 1), suggesting that cells with an increased
L134@P1: [Ca2+]cyt caused by the first stimulus are more sensitive to a second
L135@P1: stimulus. The leaf area with increased fluorescence was indistinguishable from the area that changed tissue curvature during the
L136@P1: leaf closure in a previous study19.
L137@P1: These results and the Ca2+ requirement of the snap movement9–11
L138@P1: are concordant with the previous proposal that [Ca2+]cyt increases
L139@P1: during excitation and is involved in triggering movement10. However,
L140@P1: to clarify the causality between [Ca2+]cyt and movement, future
L141@P1: genetic studies are necessary. The anisotropic differences in propagation velocities of the [Ca2+]cyt increase and the acceleration of propagation velocities in response to the second stimulus (Extended Data
L142@P1: Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 1) are qualitatively in agreement
L143@P1: with the behaviour of leaf action potentials8
L144@P1: . However, the action
L145@P1: potentials propagate at 60–170mms–1 after the first stimulus and
L146@P1: 250mms–1 after the second stimulus8,20, much faster than the propagation of [Ca2+]cyt changes (20–53mms–1 after the first stimulus,
L147@P1: 51–102mms–1 after the second stimulus; Supplementary Table 1).
L148@P1: Furthermore, lateral movement of the [Ca2+]cyt wave stops once it
L149@P1: reached the area where the secondary veins branch (Fig. 2f), while
L150@P1: action potentials continue beyond that boundary to reach the margin of the leaf blade8
L151@P1: . These results suggest that propagation of the
L152@P1: [Ca2+]cyt wave is not directly linked to that of the action potentials.
L153@P1: Since different experimental setups result in variable velocities of
L154@P1: action potentials21, a measurement of action potentials in GCaMP6f
L155@P1: Dionaea together with [Ca2+]cyt changes with an intact leaf is necessary to further investigate the relationship between [Ca2+]cyt wave and
L156@P1: action potential, although it is not possible at this stage in Dionaea.
L157@P1: To investigate whether the need for two stimuli can be explained
L158@P1: by there being a [Ca2+]cyt threshold for movement10, we quantitated
L159@P1: GCaMP6f fluorescence intensity in the lateral and central areas of
L160@P1: leaf blades (Fig. 2h) every 0.02 s after a mechanical stimulus to a sensory hair (Fig. 3a,b). We normalized fluorescence intensity at time
L161@P1: t to the maximum intensity after the first stimulus, to yield relative
L162@P1: intensity Ft

L164@P1: triggered an elevation in fluorescence intensity, which then gradually decreased in both areas of the leaf (Fig. 3a,b). Fluorescence
L165@P1: increased additively in response to the second stimulus in both
L166@P1: areas and then the leaf closed. The maximum fluorescence intensity
L167@P1: after the second stimulus was higher than that reached after the first
L168@P1: stimulus. Fluorescence intensities after the start of leaf movement
L169@P1: could not be accurately measured because of the rapid movement.

L284@P3: We also investigated whether the third stimulus can increase

L416@P4: hand, LaCl3-treated leaves did not move even after the third stimulus and [Ca2+]cyt did not reach 95% CI of the putative threshold
L417@P4: at the lateral area (Extended Data Fig. 10b, Supplementary Fig. 8b
L418@P4: and Supplementary Video 9). These results are concordant with the
L419@P4: hypothesis that leaf movement is triggered when the [Ca2+]cyt surpasses the threshold for the movement.
L420@P4: This study shows that (1) the first mechanical stimulus to a sensory hair increases [Ca2+]cyt in the leaf tissue responsible for movement, (2) the elevated [Ca2+]cyt decreases two-phase exponentially
L421@P4: after the first stimulus, (3) the second stimulus additively increases
L422@P4: [Ca2+]cyt, (4) [Ca2+]cyt meets a putative threshold for movement after
L423@P4: the second stimulus and (5) the time course of [Ca2+]cyt decay after
L424@P4: the first stimulus and the putative [Ca2+]cyt threshold for movement
L425@P4: are consistent with a memory system in Dionaea. Further studies
L426@P4: on Dionaea leaf movement will reveal the molecular mechanisms
L427@P4: of calcium dynamics to trigger movement especially on the relationships of [Ca2+]cyt change to mechanostimulus, action potentials
L428@P4: and turgor changes to trigger movement, as well as the evolution
L429@P4: of rapid movement in plants. In addition, since the leaf area with
L430@P4: increased [Ca2+]cyt corresponds to the area in which the effective
L431@P4: quantum yield of photosystem II transiently decreases after the
L432@P4: mechanical stimulus to the sensory hair22,23, studies on the relationships between [Ca2+]cyt dynamics and other physiological responses
L433@P4: will give insight into the evolution of carnivory in plants.

L486@P4: Microscopy. Stereoscopic images and videos were taken using a SZX16 (Olympus)
L487@P4: fluorescence microscope equipped with a SZX2-FGFP long-pass filter (Olympus)
L488@P4: and a digital camera DP74 (Olympus). Fluorescence videos were taken using
L489@P4: the linear mode of cellSens Standard (1.17) in a range where the fluorescence
L490@P4: intensities of samples and brightness values of captured images are linear. All
L491@P4: fluorescence movies were taken at 50 frames per second, with a 2-ms exposure
L492@P4: time (Fig. 2a, b) or 15-ms exposure time (others) and 16× gain, in linear contrast
L493@P4: mode and with 2×2 binning. Images were saved as a sequence of uncompressed
L494@P4: tiff files. Blue, green and red channels were split from the original images and only
L495@P4: green channel images were used for the analysis. All fluorescence images were
L496@P4: pseudocoloured with green or LUT (fire lookup table) in ImageJ (1.52p). All videos
L497@P4: were constructed from the green channel images of the original uncompressed
L498@P4: tiff images. The time course of the two-dimensional propagation of increased
L499@P4: fluorescence was determined by manually connecting the boundaries of fluorescent
L500@P4: areas (Fig. 2d,e). To calculate the propagation velocity of the [Ca2+]cyt increase,
L501@P4: leaves and petioles were considered to be flat planes and the velocity induced by
L502@P4: the stimulus was measured 0.04 s (Extended Data Fig. 3a,c), 0.02 s (Extended Data
L503@P4: Fig. 3b) and 5 s (Extended Data Fig. 3d) after the stimulus. To compare the areas
L504@P4: with increased [Ca2+]cyt after application of the first and second stimuli, the pixel
L505@P4: intensity distribution was classified into two distributions: pixels with large changes
L506@P4: and pixels with small changes in intensity. Pixels with small changes were set as
L507@P4: background and were assigned the same value in images acquired after the first and
